prompt.1: What should schools teach about gender and different kinds of families?
prompt.2: Some BC schools use SOGI 123, teaching materials about sexual orientation, gender identity and families. What should the province do?
prompt.3: Should the province repeal, step back from, keep or expand SOGI 123, optional school materials on sexual orientation and gender identity?
prompt.4: SOGI 123 (sexual orientation and gender identity) is optional and chosen by each school district, and provincial funding for its creator ends in 2026-27. What should BC do?
prompt.5: SOGI 123 is an optional, district-selected sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) resource from the ARC Foundation (2016). Choose the provincial stance you support.

context.1: Some schools use lessons about gender and different kinds of families. Each school district decides whether to use them. The government is ending its funding for the group that made them. Everyone wants kids safe at school. People disagree on who should choose these lessons.
context.2: SOGI 123 is a set of optional teaching materials about sexual orientation and gender identity. Each school district chooses whether to use it. Supporters say it reduces bullying. Critics say families should decide what children learn about gender. The province is ending its funding for the group that created it.
context.3: SOGI 123 is an optional set of school materials on sexual orientation and gender identity, first released in 2016. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal it. The NDP government is ending funding for the group that created it but keeps anti-bullying work. The Greens support it 'unequivocally'. CentreBC opposes repealing anti-discrimination protections but has not committed to SOGI 123.
context.4: SOGI 123 is optional, and each district chooses whether to use it. The Conservatives would repeal it but have not said how they would end a resource that is not required. OneBC would also pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Premier Eby says 'it's up to the teachers'. The Greens would expand it. CentreBC opposes repealing rights protections. Pronoun rules and parental notification are not scored, because the parties have no 2026 positions on them.
context.5: The Conservative plan says it would repeal SOGI but names no mechanism. Its 2024 platform promised to remove SOGI-derived lesson plans, a zero-tolerance anti-bullying policy and parental notification of suicidal intent. The NDP government cut ARC Foundation funding from $350,000 to $0 by 2026-27, and the ministry says the resources stay online. OneBC's bill on pronouns and puberty blockers was defeated 48 to 40. The Greens would expand SOGI 123 and fund one counsellor per 250 students. CentreBC would not repeal anti-discrimination law. The Human Rights Code has covered gender identity since 2016.

text.1: This party keeps the laws against discrimination but is ending funding for the group that made the lessons. Teachers choose.
text.3: The NDP government is ending funding for the ARC Foundation, which created SOGI 123. It says the materials stay online, districts choose, and anti-bullying work continues. In 2024 it passed a law creating zones around schools where disruptive protest is an offence. It has no 2026 platform item on SOGI.
text.5: The NDP cut ARC Foundation funding from $350,000 (2024-25) to $200,000 (2025-26) to $0 (2026-27), citing 'expenditure management'; the ministry says SOGI 123 is 'not defunded' and stays online. Its Safe Access to Schools Act (2024) created access zones within 20 metres of schools where disrupting or intimidating students and staff is an offence. Eby says it is 'up to the teachers'. It voted against the gender-identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills and has no position on pronouns, parental notification or athletes.

text.1: This party wants all lessons on gender identity out of schools, with parents deciding at home.
text.3: OneBC would repeal SOGI 123, 'remove all gender ideology content' from classrooms, and pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Its bill to stop puberty blockers for minors and to bar use of the 'wrong pronoun' in schools was defeated.
text.5: OneBC would repeal SOGI 123, remove gender ideology content and pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Its October 2025 bill, Tara Armstrong's Protecting Minors from Gender Transition Act, to stop puberty blockers for minors, bar wrong-pronoun use and ban public funds for transition was defeated 48 to 40. Armstrong left OneBC in December 2025; her February 2026 Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act, which Brodie voted for, was defeated 38 to 49. It is not running candidates against eight Conservatives who share its views on SOGI.

scoring_rationale: Four options. a = OneBC (4); Conservatives 3 given the 2024 pledge to strip SOGI-derived materials, short of a Parental Bill of Rights in 2026. b = Conservative 2026 text (4); OneBC 3. c = the keep-protections, districts-choose, no-provincial-program position: NDP 4 on its record (kept the Human Rights Code and anti-bullying policy, cut ARC funding to $0, left districts to choose) and CentreBC 4 on its stated stance (opposes repeal of any anti-discrimination law, affirms inclusion, platform silent on SOGI 123); the two differ in tone, not in stated policy, so they score alike. Green 2 (keeps protections, wants more); Conservative 1 (its plan keeps the Code and ends the program); OneBC 0. d = Green (4); CentreBC 1 (no commitment to fund or expand SOGI 123; its 1-per-400 counsellor pledge is general school staffing, not a SOGI measure; lowered from 2 on October 12 after a reader pointed this out); NDP 1 because the budget cut the funding regardless of campaign framing (record over rhetoric). First-reading votes on the 2026 private members' bills are described in the party records and positions but are not scored, consistent with the DRIPA question.
